blurb: How text becomes numbers an AI can work with: chopping words into tokens, turning meaning into a map, and searching by meaning.

steps.p: A neural network can only do maths on numbers. So before a model sees your message, the text is chopped into pieces called tokens, and each piece gets an ID number.
Common words are one token; rarer words are split into parts. Roughly, 1 token ≈ ¾ of an English word.

visual.caption: Illustration: each piece gets an ID number.

steps.p: Tokens usually include the space before a word, so "hello" and " hello" are different tokens.

The token list is built by starting with single characters and repeatedly merging the most common pairs ("t"+"h" → "th", "th"+"e" → "the")… until there are tens of thousands of tokens. This is byte-pair encoding.
Modern tokenizers work on raw bytes, so any text — emoji, any language — can be encoded, even if just as small fragments.

cards.q: As a rule of thumb for English, 1,000 tokens is about how many words?
cards.why: About 750. That's why a 200,000-token context window holds roughly 150,000 words.

cards.statement: "hello" and " hello" (with a space in front) are usually the same token.
cards.why: False. The space is usually part of the token, so they get different IDs. Small details like this can quietly affect model behaviour.

cards.q: Byte-pair encoding starts from single characters and then…
options: Repeatedly merges the most common neighbouring pair into a new token
cards.why: Merges common pairs. Frequent chunks like "the" or "ing" become single tokens, so common text is short and efficient.

cards.title: The same sentence can cost several times more tokens in some languages than in English.
cards.detail: Tokenizers trained mostly on English split other scripts into small fragments. Studies found gaps of several-fold — meaning higher costs and less room in the context window.

cards.statement: Byte-level tokenizers can encode any text at all, including emoji and unfamiliar scripts.
cards.why: True. Every text is ultimately bytes, and every byte is in the vocabulary. Unfamiliar text just uses more tokens.

steps.h: A list of numbers per token
steps.p: Each token ID is swapped for an embedding: a long list of numbers (often thousands) that the model learned during training.
Picture each embedding as a point on a giant map. Words with similar meanings end up near each other: "cat" near "kitten", far from "tax".
steps.analogy: Like a city where all the bakeries cluster in one neighbourhood and all the banks in another.

steps.p: Directions on the map can carry meaning. Famously: king − man + woman lands near queen.
Cosine similarity measures whether two embeddings point the same way: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated, −1 = opposite.
Inside a transformer, attention updates each embedding using the words around it, so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank loan" end up in different places.

cards.q: The famous "king − man + woman ≈ queen" result came from which 2013 model?
cards.why: word2vec, from Google. It showed that simple training on text produces embeddings where directions carry meaning.

cards.q: On the embedding map, which word would sit closest to "kitten"?
cards.why: cat. Words used in similar ways in text end up with similar embeddings, so they sit close together on the map.

cards.q: Cosine similarity between two embeddings ranges from…
cards.why: −1 to 1. It measures the angle between two arrows: same direction, unrelated, or opposite.

cards.title: Inside a transformer, "bank" gets different embeddings in "river bank" and "bank loan".
cards.detail: word2vec gave each word one fixed embedding. Transformers start from one, but attention mixes in context, so by the middle layers the two meanings are far apart.

cards.statement: Some language models reuse their input embeddings in their output layer.
cards.why: True. Called weight tying: the same table that turns tokens into embeddings is used to score which token comes next. It saves parameters.

steps.p: A special embedding model turns a whole sentence or paragraph into one embedding that sums up its meaning.
It's trained on matching pairs (a question and its answer) to pull matches together and push non-matches apart.
Embed your question, then find the passages whose embeddings are closest to it.

items: Compare with millions of stored embeddings

steps.p: Comparing against millions one by one is slow, so search indexes like HNSW jump through a map of neighbours, trading a tiny chance of a miss for a huge speedup.
steps.analogy: Finding a house by asking directions from neighbourhood to street, rather than knocking on every door.

steps.p: Embeddings can blur exact names, codes and rare terms, so good systems mix in keyword search too.

cards.statement: The embedding model used for search is usually the same model as the chatbot.
cards.why: False. Search usually uses a smaller, specialised embedding model trained for matching meaning.

cards.q: Fast search indexes like HNSW give up what in exchange for speed?
options: A small chance of missing the true closest match
cards.hint: Asking directions vs knocking on every door.
cards.why: A tiny chance of a miss. In return, searching millions of embeddings takes milliseconds instead of seconds.

cards.title: Some embedding models let you chop their embeddings shorter and still use them.
cards.detail: "Matryoshka" training puts the most important information in the first numbers. OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models support this, saving storage.

cards.statement: Embeddings from two different embedding models can be compared with each other directly.
cards.why: False. Each model draws its own map. Comparing points from two maps is meaningless — like using one city's map to navigate another.

cards.q: Why do many search systems mix embeddings with old-fashioned keyword search?
options: Keyword search catches exact names, codes and rare terms that embeddings can blur
cards.why: Exact matches. Searching "error E-4021" needs the exact code, which meaning-based search may treat as similar to other codes.

steps.p: A model sees "strawberry" as maybe 2–3 tokens, not 10 letters. Spelling and letter-counting are surprisingly hard for it.

visual.caption: Illustration: how many r's? The model has to remember what's inside each chunk.

steps.p: Some tokenizers split "12345" into chunks like "123" and "45", which makes arithmetic harder. Others use single digits.
More tokens in the vocabulary means shorter sequences (cheaper) but a bigger embedding table and more rarely seen tokens.
Tokens that were in the vocabulary but almost never in training data barely learned anything, and can make models act strangely.
Asking a model to spell a word out letter by letter first lets each letter become its own token, fixing many of these issues.
steps.analogy: Like sounding a word out before counting its letters.

cards.q: Why have chatbots historically struggled to count the r's in "strawberry"?
options: They see a few tokens, not individual letters
cards.hint: Look at the cells in step 1.
cards.why: Tokens, not letters. The model must recall what letters are inside each chunk. Spelling it out first makes it easy.

cards.title: "SolidGoldMagikarp" was a token that made GPT-3 behave bizarrely.
cards.detail: It came from a Reddit username, so it was in the vocabulary, but almost never appeared in training. Its embedding was barely trained, and asking about it produced strange replies.

cards.statement: All chatbot tokenizers split numbers into single digits.
cards.why: False. Some do; others group digits into chunks. The choice noticeably affects how well models do arithmetic.

cards.q: What's the main trade-off of a larger vocabulary?
options: Shorter sequences, but a bigger embedding table and more rarely seen tokens
It makes the model forget words
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 3.
cards.why: Cheaper sequences, bigger table. Labs balance the two; vocabularies have grown as models got bigger.

cards.title: Meta's Llama 3 quadrupled its vocabulary from 32,000 to 128,000 tokens.
cards.detail: Meta reported this encoded the same text with up to 15% fewer tokens, making it cheaper to run and fitting more into the context window.

cards.title: See your text the way a model does
cards.body: Free tokenizer tools on the web show exactly how text gets chopped into tokens.
cards.challenge: Search for "OpenAI tokenizer", paste a sentence, and see how many tokens it uses. Try a long word and a number too.
